q.s: A 10-month-old boy of Cypriot descent has pallor, poor feeding and an enlarging abdomen. He was well until 6 months of age. He has frontal bossing and maxillary overgrowth, and the liver and spleen are enlarged. Skull x-ray shows a "hair-on-end" pattern. His laboratory results are shown.
e: Wrong. Not the main treatment complication.
Correct. β-thalassemia major (β0/β0) needs regular transfusions, causing iron overload; chelation is required.
cl: He was well until 6 months of age
the liver and spleen are enlarged
q.ch: Mediterranean infant + onset after 6 months + marrow expansion + absent HbA, high HbF (table) → β-thalassemia major → transfusions → iron overload.
q.tr: β-thal major becomes symptomatic as γ chains switch off.
q.q2: This child is at greatest long-term risk of which complication of his treatment?

head: Test
Result
Reference
rows: Target cells, marked anisopoikilocytosis, nucleated RBCs

q.s: A 30-year-old woman of Southeast Asian descent has lifelong moderate anemia and splenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL with an MCV of 61 fL. Smear shows target cells. Supravital staining shows many red cells with multiple small inclusions giving a "golf ball" appearance. Electrophoresis shows a fast-moving abnormal band.
e: Correct. Hemoglobin H disease: excess β chains form β4 tetramers that precipitate.
q.ch: Asian ancestry + moderate microcytic hemolytic anemia + HbH inclusions → 3 α-gene deletions → HbH (β4).
q.tr: α deletions: 1 silent, 2 trait, 3 HbH (β4), 4 Barts (γ4).
q.q2: How many α-globin genes are most likely deleted?

q.s: A 25-year-old African American woman has occasional episodes of bone pain and mild anemia. She had splenic infarction during an airplane flight. Hemoglobin is 11.4 g/dL. Her hemoglobin electrophoresis (lane 3) is shown with control lanes. In each lane, bands closer to the wells (origin, cathode) are, from top to bottom: HbC, HbS, HbF, HbA.
e: Wrong. No HbC band; usually more severe anemia.
Correct. One HbS and one HbC allele; milder than HbSS.
cl: High prevalence of HbS and HbC.
splenic infarction during an airplane flight
q.ch: Mild sickling disease + bands at HbS and HbC positions, no HbA (figure) → HbSC disease.
q.tr: HbC (lysine) is closest to the cathode; HbA is farthest.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 7-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has a 3-day history of fever and a lacy red rash that began on his cheeks. He is now very pale and tired. His laboratory results are shown alongside his usual values.
o: Parvovirus B19 infection of erythroid precursors
e: Wrong. The spleen would enlarge and reticulocytes would rise.
Correct. Aplastic crisis: transient arrest of erythropoiesis; reticulocytes fall to near zero.
Wrong. WBC and platelets are normal.
cl: lacy red rash that began on his cheeks
He is now very pale and tired
q.ch: Sickle cell disease + slapped-cheek rash + sharp Hb fall with reticulocytes near zero, normal WBC/platelets (table) → parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis.
q.tr: Low reticulocytes in a hemolytic anemia = aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19).
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

q.s: An 18-year-old man with sickle cell disease is seen for routine care. A peripheral smear shows small, round, dark purple inclusions in many red cells. The spleen cannot be palpated or seen on ultrasound.
e: Correct. Howell-Jolly bodies indicate autosplenectomy; patients are at risk from encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, H. influenzae, meningococcus, Salmonella).
cl: The spleen cannot be palpated or seen on ultrasound
q.ch: Sickle cell disease → splenic infarction → autosplenectomy → Howell-Jolly bodies → risk of encapsulated organisms → vaccinate.
q.tr: Howell-Jolly bodies = no functioning spleen.
q.q2: Which of the following is most important for preventing life-threatening complications related to this finding?

q.s: A 52-year-old man who drinks a liter of wine daily and eats poorly has fatigue. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL. Neutrophils show 6 to 7 nuclear lobes. Neurologic examination is normal. Serum homocysteine is elevated; methylmalonic acid is normal.
e: Correct. Malnutrition from alcohol; elevated homocysteine with normal MMA and no neurologic findings.
Wrong. MMA would be high, often neurologic signs.
cl: drinks a liter of wine daily and eats poorly
q.ch: Malnourished drinker + megaloblastic anemia + high homocysteine, normal MMA, no neuro → folate deficiency.
q.tr: Folate: weeks to deplete; B12: years.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his anemia?

q.s: A 14-month-old girl has failure to thrive and delayed walking. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL with an MCV of 109 fL and hypersegmented neutrophils. Treatment with folate and vitamin B12 for 2 months has not helped. Serum ammonia is normal. Urine contains large amounts of orotic acid.
e: Correct. Orotic aciduria: UMP synthase defect; uridine bypasses the block.
Wrong. Urea cycle defects with hyperammonemia.
cl: failure to thrive and delayed walking
q.ch: Child + megaloblastic anemia refractory to B12/folate + orotic aciduria without hyperammonemia → UMP synthase defect → uridine.
q.tr: Orotic acid + high ammonia = OTC deficiency; orotic acid + normal ammonia = orotic aciduria.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

q.s: A 5-month-old boy has pallor and poor feeding. He has a small head, widely spaced eyes and a thumb with three bones. Hemoglobin is 5.9 g/dL with an MCV of 106 fL. Reticulocytes are 0.1%. WBC and platelet counts are normal. HbF is elevated.
e: Correct. Congenital pure red cell aplasia with triphalangeal thumbs, onset in the first year.
cl: WBC and platelet counts are normal
q.ch: Infant + macrocytic anemia, very low reticulocytes + normal WBC/platelets + thumb anomaly → Diamond-Blackfan.
q.tr: "A pure Diamond causes pure red cell aplasia."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: An 8-year-old boy is short for his age and has café-au-lait spots, a hypoplastic thumb and an absent radius on the left. He has recurrent nosebleeds and infections. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL, WBC count is 2,200/mm³ and platelets are 31,000/mm³. Bone marrow is hypocellular.
e: Correct. Fanconi anemia: autosomal recessive DNA repair defect causing marrow failure and cancer predisposition.
q.ch: Short stature + café-au-lait + radial ray defects + pancytopenia → Fanconi anemia → DNA repair defect.
q.tr: Fanconi = pancytopenia; Diamond-Blackfan = red cells only.
q.q2: Which cellular process is defective?

q.s: A 2-day-old girl of Amish descent has jaundice and anemia. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL with reticulocytes of 14%. The smear shows red cells with small, evenly spaced projections. The direct antiglobulin test is negative and G6PD activity is normal.
o: Decreased ATP making red cells rigid
e: Correct. Pyruvate kinase deficiency: autosomal recessive; burr cells and extravascular hemolysis in a newborn.
cl: A population with increased PK deficiency.
direct antiglobulin test is negative and G6PD activity is normal
q.ch: Newborn + Coombs-negative hemolysis + burr cells + normal G6PD → PK deficiency → low ATP, rigid RBCs.
q.tr: PK deficiency also raises 2,3-BPG, shifting the O2 curve right.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains the red cell injury?

q.s: A 30-year-old man of West African descent has mild anemia and an enlarged spleen. He has never had pain crises. Smear shows many target cells and some red cells containing dense rod-shaped crystals.
o: Point mutation in a splice site
e: Correct. HbC disease: target cells and intracellular crystals, extravascular hemolysis.
cl: HbC is common in West Africa.
q.ch: West African ancestry + mild hemolysis + target cells + crystals → homozygous HbC → glutamic acid to lysine.
q.tr: Target cells: "HALT" — HbC, Asplenia, Liver disease, Thalassemia.
q.q2: Which amino acid substitution in β-globin is most likely present on both alleles?

q.s: A 64-year-old man had a mechanical aortic valve replacement 8 years ago. He now has fatigue and dark urine. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL, LDH is 980 U/L and haptoglobin is undetectable. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. A new paravalvular leak is seen on echocardiography.
e: Correct. Macroangiopathic (mechanical) hemolysis from a prosthetic valve.
q.ch: Mechanical valve with leak + Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis → mechanical fragmentation → schistocytes.
q.tr: Schistocytes = MAHA (DIC, TTP/HUS, HELLP) or mechanical valves.
q.q2: Which finding is expected on the peripheral smear?

q.s: A 26-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, weakness in her arms and anxiety. The current episode began after she started a strict diet and took a friend's barbiturate to sleep. Abdominal examination is benign. Her urine turns dark red when left in sunlight.
e: Correct. Acute intermittent porphyria (porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency).
cl: strict diet and took a friend's barbiturate
Starvation and CYP450 inducers raise ALA synthase.
dark red when left in sunlight
q.ch: 5 P's + precipitants (fasting, barbiturate) + benign abdomen → AIP → PBG and ALA in urine.
q.tr: AIP: Painful abdomen, Port-wine Pee, Polyneuropathy, Psychological disturbance, Precipitated by drugs.
q.q2: Which substance accumulates in her urine?

q.s: A 55-year-old man with hepatitis C has fragile skin and blisters on the backs of his hands that heal with scarring. He has increased facial hair and darkened skin. He drinks heavily. His urine is tea-colored.
e: Correct. Porphyria cutanea tarda (uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase); hydroxychloroquine is also used.
cl: blisters on the backs of his hands
q.ch: HCV + alcohol + photosensitive blisters + hyperpigmentation + tea-colored urine → PCT → phlebotomy.
q.tr: PCT is the most common porphyria and is the "skin" one; AIP is the "nerve and belly" one.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

q.s: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after swallowing many of his pregnant mother's iron tablets. He has vomiting and bloody diarrhea. Abdominal x-ray shows multiple radiopaque tablets in the stomach.
e: Correct. Iron chelator for acute iron poisoning.
cl: Adult iron pills look like candy.
q.ch: Child + iron ingestion + GI bleeding + radiopaque pills → acute iron poisoning → deferoxamine.
q.tr: Iron and other heavy metals are radiopaque; charcoal does not bind iron.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate antidote?

q.s: A 5-week-old breastfed boy born at home is brought in with oozing from his umbilical stump and a bulging fontanelle. He received no medications after birth. Platelet count is normal. PT and PTT are both markedly prolonged.
e: Correct. Newborns lack vitamin K–producing gut bacteria; vitamin K deficiency bleeding is prevented by a dose at birth.
cl: Breast milk is low in vitamin K.
He received no medications after birth
PT and PTT are both markedly prolonged
Deficiency of II, VII, IX and X.
q.ch: Newborn without vitamin K + breastfed + bleeding with prolonged PT and PTT, normal platelets → vitamin K deficiency → prevent with vitamin K at birth.
q.tr: Neonates lack enteric "baKteria" that make vitamin K.
q.q2: Which of the following would most likely have prevented this?

q.s: A 9-year-old boy has frequent nosebleeds. His parents are first cousins. Platelet count is 105,000/mm³ and the smear shows very large platelets. Bleeding time is prolonged. Platelets aggregate normally with ADP but fail to agglutinate with ristocetin, and adding normal plasma does not correct it.
e: Wrong. ADP receptor; aggregation with ADP is normal.
Wrong. Would correct with normal plasma.
Correct. Bernard-Soulier syndrome: autosomal recessive defect in adhesion to vWF; big platelets.
cl: adding normal plasma does not correct it
q.ch: AR + mucosal bleeding + giant platelets + ristocetin defect not corrected by plasma → Bernard-Soulier → GpIb deficiency.
q.tr: Bernard-Soulier = Big platelets, GpIb.
q.q2: Which platelet glycoprotein is deficient?

q.s: A 6-year-old girl has had easy bruising and gum bleeding since infancy. Platelet count and size are normal. Bleeding time is prolonged. Ristocetin agglutination is normal, but platelets do not aggregate in response to ADP, collagen or thrombin. Platelets do not clump on the smear.
e: Correct. GpIIb/IIIa deficiency: platelets cannot bind fibrinogen to aggregate.
Wrong. Not since infancy; ADP aggregation partly preserved.
cl: Platelet count and size are normal
Platelets do not clump on the smear
q.ch: Lifelong mucosal bleeding + normal count + normal ristocetin + absent aggregation to all agonists → Glanzmann (GpIIb/IIIa).
q.tr: Glanzmann = no Gluing platelets together (GpIIb/IIIa).
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 58-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease on irregular dialysis needs a kidney biopsy. He has a history of prolonged bleeding after minor cuts. Platelet count, PT and PTT are normal.
o: Uremic toxins impairing platelet adhesion and aggregation
e: Correct. Uremic platelet dysfunction; desmopressin and dialysis improve it.
cl: end-stage kidney disease on irregular dialysis
Platelet count, PT and PTT are normal
q.ch: Uremia + bleeding with normal count and coagulation tests → uremic platelet dysfunction.
q.tr: Normal counts and clotting tests do not exclude a platelet function problem.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains his bleeding tendency?

q.s: A 67-year-old woman with urosepsis is in the ICU. She develops oozing from catheter sites and petechiae. Her coagulation results are shown with those of two other patients for comparison.
o: Widespread activation and consumption of clotting factors and platelets
e: Wrong. TTP (like patient X); normal PT/PTT.
Correct. DIC: low platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT/PTT, high D-dimer, schistocytes.
Wrong. Like patient Y; normal platelets and fibrinogen.
Wrong. D-dimer would not be this high and schistocytes absent.
cl: Sepsis is a major cause of DIC.
q.ch: Sepsis + bleeding + low platelets, prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, schistocytes (table) → DIC.
q.tr: DIC: everything abnormal; TTP/HUS: normal PT/PTT; vitamin K deficiency: normal platelets.
q.q2: Which of the following best describes the process in this patient?

q.s: A 40-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome develops a left renal vein thrombosis. He is started on a standard dose of unfractionated heparin. After 24 hours his PTT has barely risen despite dose increases.
o: Loss of antithrombin in the urine
e: Wrong. Causes low platelets, not heparin resistance.
Correct. Heparin works through antithrombin; nephrotic syndrome causes acquired antithrombin deficiency.
Wrong. Does not affect heparin response.
q.ch: Nephrotic syndrome → urinary antithrombin loss → thrombosis + heparin resistance.
q.tr: Antithrombin deficiency blunts the PTT rise after heparin.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains his poor response to heparin?

q.s: A 72-year-old man without prior bleeding problems develops large bruises on his arms and a thigh hematoma. Platelet count is normal. Results of coagulation studies are shown.
e: Wrong. Congenital; would correct with mixing.
Correct. A prolonged PTT that does not correct with mixing (worsens with incubation) and low factor VIII indicates an autoantibody against factor VIII, the most common acquired inhibitor.
cl: large bruises on his arms and a thigh hematoma
q.ch: New bleeding in an older adult + isolated prolonged PTT that does not correct on mixing + low factor VIII (table) → acquired factor VIII inhibitor.
q.tr: Mixing corrects = deficiency; does not correct = inhibitor.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

head: Test
Result
Reference
rows: PTT after 1:1 mix with normal plasma (immediate)

q.s: A 25-year-old man with multiple gunshot wounds receives 14 units of packed RBCs in 2 hours. He develops perioral tingling, muscle twitching and hypotension. ECG shows a prolonged QT interval.
o: Hypocalcemia from citrate in stored blood
e: Wrong. Peaked T waves, not QT prolongation.
Correct. Citrate chelates calcium during massive transfusion.
cl: 14 units of packed RBCs in 2 hours
q.ch: Massive transfusion → citrate load → hypocalcemia → tetany, hypotension, long QT.
q.tr: Citrate is the anticoagulant in stored blood and binds calcium.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains these findings?

q.s: A 66-year-old man has fatigue, night sweats and diffuse lymphadenopathy. Colonoscopy shows multiple polyps that are lymphoma on biopsy. The tumor cells are CD5-positive, CD23-negative B cells that strongly express cyclin D1.
e: Correct. Mantle cell lymphoma: cyclin D1, CD5+, usually late stage.
q.ch: Older man + widespread disease + CD5+/CD23− + cyclin D1 → mantle cell lymphoma → t(11;14), aggressive.
q.tr: CD5+ B-cell tumors: CLL (CD23+) and mantle cell (CD23−, cyclin D1).
q.q2: Which of the following is most likely?

q.s: A 62-year-old woman has epigastric pain. Endoscopy shows a thickened gastric mucosa. Biopsy shows small atypical lymphocytes infiltrating gastric glands, with curved gram-negative rods on the surface. The disease is confined to the stomach wall.
e: Correct. Gastric MALT (marginal zone) lymphoma often regresses after H. pylori eradication.
cl: small atypical lymphocytes infiltrating gastric glands
q.ch: Gastric lymphoma + H. pylori + localized → MALT lymphoma → H. pylori eradication.
q.tr: MALT lymphoma: chronic inflammation (H. pylori, Sjögren, Hashimoto).
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

q.s: A 38-year-old man with AIDS (CD4 count 34/mm³) has 3 weeks of confusion and memory loss. MRI shows a single ring-enhancing periventricular lesion. Toxoplasma IgG is negative. CSF PCR detects Epstein-Barr virus DNA.
e: Wrong. JC virus, nonenhancing white matter lesions.
q.ch: AIDS + solitary ring-enhancing lesion + negative toxo serology + EBV in CSF → primary CNS lymphoma.
q.tr: AIDS + single lesion + EBV = lymphoma; multiple lesions + toxo IgG = toxoplasmosis.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 50-year-old man from Jamaica has skin plaques, generalized lymphadenopathy and confusion. Calcium is 13.6 mg/dL and x-rays show lytic bone lesions. Smear shows lymphocytes with cloverleaf-shaped nuclei that are CD4-positive T cells.
e: Correct. Adult T-cell lymphoma (Japan, West Africa, Caribbean).
cl: Calcium is 13.6 mg/dL and x-rays show lytic bone lesions
q.ch: Caribbean origin + skin lesions + hypercalcemia + lytic bones + CD4+ T cells → adult T-cell lymphoma → HTLV-1.
q.tr: "T-cell in Tokyo" — HTLV in Japan, Caribbean, West Africa.
q.q2: Which of the following is the cause of this malignancy?

q.s: A 64-year-old man has had red, scaly patches on his buttocks and trunk for years that are now thickening into plaques. Skin biopsy shows atypical CD4-positive T cells collecting in clusters within the epidermis.
e: Correct. The most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma; patches → plaques → tumors in sun-protected areas.
cl: red, scaly patches on his buttocks and trunk
atypical CD4-positive T cells collecting in clusters within the epidermis
q.ch: Chronic patches in sun-protected skin progressing to plaques + epidermotropic CD4+ T cells → mycosis fungoides.
q.tr: Mycosis fungoides is a T-cell lymphoma, not a fungus.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 74-year-old man treated with chemotherapy and radiation for lymphoma 6 years ago has fatigue and infections. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL with an MCV of 104 fL, WBC count is 2,800/mm³ and platelets are 72,000/mm³. The smear shows neutrophils with bilobed nuclei. The marrow is hypercellular with dysplasia in all myeloid lines and 8% blasts.
e: Correct. Myelodysplastic syndrome (blasts <20%) can transform to AML.
q.ch: Older adult + prior chemo/radiation + cytopenias + dysplasia + blasts <20% → MDS → risk of AML.
q.tr: Blasts ≥20% = AML; <20% with dysplasia = MDS.
q.q2: Which of the following is this patient at greatest risk of developing?

q.s: A 16-year-old boy has a 2-week history of facial swelling and shortness of breath when lying flat. His neck veins are distended. Chest x-ray shows a large anterior mediastinal mass. WBC count is 62,000/mm³ with many blasts that are TdT-positive and CD3-positive.
e: Wrong. TdT and CD3 are lymphoid markers.
Wrong. RS cells, not circulating TdT+ blasts.
Correct. Presents as a mediastinal (thymic) mass with SVC-like syndrome.
cl: facial swelling and shortness of breath when lying flat
q.ch: Adolescent + anterior mediastinal mass + SVC syndrome + TdT+, CD3+ blasts → T-ALL.
q.tr: B-ALL: CD10, CD19; T-ALL: CD3, mediastinal mass.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed AML has a WBC count of 210,000/mm³ with myeloblasts. He becomes confused and short of breath, and his oxygen saturation falls. Chest x-ray shows diffuse infiltrates.
e: Correct. Large, rigid blasts plug capillaries in the brain and lungs.
Wrong. Less likely with this picture.
q.ch: AML + very high blast count + neurologic and pulmonary symptoms → leukostasis.
q.tr: Leukostasis is a medical emergency in AML with very high WBC.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains his symptoms?

q.s: A 49-year-old woman has headaches and burning pain with redness in her fingers. She bled heavily after a minor procedure. Hemoglobin and WBC count are normal. Platelet count is 1,350,000/mm³. Iron studies are normal and there is no inflammation. Testing for BCR-ABL is negative; a JAK2 mutation is found.
e: Correct. Massive platelet proliferation with bleeding and thrombosis, erythromelalgia; JAK2 in 30–50%.
Wrong. Normal iron and no inflammation; JAK2 positive.
cl: burning pain with redness in her fingers
Hemoglobin and WBC count are normal
q.ch: Isolated marked thrombocytosis + bleeding/erythromelalgia + no reactive cause + JAK2 → essential thrombocythemia.
q.tr: Very high platelets can bleed because large vWF multimers are adsorbed.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: Three patients are evaluated for an elevated hematocrit. Patient 2 has a flank mass. Their plasma volume, oxygen saturation and erythropoietin levels are shown.
o: Inappropriate absolute polycythemia from EPO-secreting tumor
e: Correct. Normal O2 with high EPO and a renal mass suggests renal cell carcinoma.
cl: These separate hypoxic, tumor-driven and primary causes.
q.ch: High Hct + normal O2 saturation + high EPO + renal mass (table) → inappropriate EPO secretion → renal cell carcinoma.
q.tr: Low O2 + high EPO = appropriate; normal O2 + high EPO = inappropriate; low EPO = PV.
q.q2: Which of the following best describes patient 2?

q.s: A 70-year-old man with severe pneumonia has a WBC count of 58,000/mm³. His smear and tests are shown.
e: Correct. Reactive neutrophilia >50,000 with toxic changes and a high LAP score.
Wrong. Would have low LAP, basophilia and BCR-ABL.
cl: Older age does not exclude a reactive cause.
q.ch: Severe infection + very high WBC with left shift + toxic granulation, Döhle bodies + high LAP + no BCR-ABL, no basophilia (table) → leukemoid reaction.
q.tr: Leukemoid reaction: LAP high; CML: LAP low.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his leukocytosis?

q.s: Warfarin is started in a patient. The plasma activities of several vitamin K–dependent proteins over the following days are shown.
o: Factor II falls faster than protein C
Protein C falls before factor II, causing a transient hypercoagulable state
Factor VII falls slowly, so PT does not change
e: Wrong. The figure shows the opposite.
Correct. Protein C has a short half-life, but factor II (the longest half-life) falls slowly, so true anticoagulation lags.
Wrong. Factor VII falls first and PT rises early.
cl: II, VII, IX, X, C, S.
q.ch: Factor VII falls first (PT rises), protein C falls early, factor II falls slowly (figure) → early hypercoagulability → heparin bridge.
q.tr: Factor VII: shortest half-life; factor II: longest ("too long").
q.q2: Which of the following best explains why heparin is given together with warfarin for the first several days?

q.s: A 78-year-old woman taking dabigatran for atrial fibrillation falls and has a subdural hematoma requiring emergency surgery.
e: Correct. Monoclonal antibody Fab fragment that binds dabigatran.
q.ch: Dabigatran + life-threatening bleed → idarucizumab.
q.tr: Heparin → protamine; warfarin → vitamin K + PCC; dabigatran → idarucizumab; Xa inhibitors → andexanet.
q.q2: Which of the following agents should be given to reverse the anticoagulant?

q.s: A 19-year-old man with osteosarcoma receives high-dose methotrexate. Two days later he has painful mouth ulcers, and his WBC count falls to 1,100/mm³.
e: Correct. Folinic acid bypasses dihydrofolate reductase ("leucovorin rescue").
Wrong. Needs DHFR to be activated, which is blocked.
q.ch: High-dose methotrexate → DHFR blocked → mucositis + myelosuppression → leucovorin rescue.
q.tr: Leucovorin rescues methotrexate but enhances 5-FU.
q.q2: Which of the following should have been given to reduce this toxicity?

q.s: A 6-year-old girl being treated for ALL has tingling in her feet, foot drop and severe constipation without fever. Her blood counts are near normal.
e: Correct. Inhibits microtubule polymerization; causes axonal neuropathy and constipation/ileus with little myelosuppression.
cl: tingling in her feet, foot drop
q.ch: ALL therapy + neuropathy + constipation with preserved counts → vincristine.
q.tr: Vincristine "crisps the nerves"; vinblastine "blasts the marrow."
q.q2: Which drug in her regimen is most likely responsible?

q.s: A 28-year-old man is treated for metastatic testicular cancer with a regimen containing a drug that cross-links DNA. He develops ringing in his ears, high-frequency hearing loss and a rising creatinine.
e: Correct. A free radical scavenger that protects against cisplatin nephrotoxicity.
q.ch: Testicular cancer + DNA cross-linker + ototoxicity + nephrotoxicity → cisplatin → amifostine.
q.tr: Cisplatin: ears, kidneys, nerves.
q.q2: Which of the following could have reduced the kidney toxicity?

q.s: A 48-year-old woman with breast cancer has a tumor that overexpresses a growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase. After 4 months of a monoclonal antibody against this receptor, she has dyspnea on exertion and her ejection fraction has fallen from 62% to 38%. She has never received anthracyclines. Three months after the drug is stopped, her ejection fraction returns to 58%.
e: Wrong. Not an antibody; often irreversible.
Wrong. VEGF; bleeding, clots, poor wound healing.
Correct. Anti-HER2 antibody; cardiomyopathy that is often reversible.
cl: overexpresses a growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase
ejection fraction has fallen from 62% to 38%
q.ch: HER2+ breast cancer + monoclonal antibody + reversible cardiomyopathy → trastuzumab.
q.tr: "Don't Trast HER, she will break your heart."
q.q2: Which drug did she most likely receive?
